patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox; Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged); Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school); Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's; Ballarat → Sydney: Fr Gerald Ridsdale.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer (Adass Israel School): first report 2008, first action 2021 (13 years). The school flew her to Israel in March 2008 before police were told; Israeli Deputy Health Minister Yaakov Litzman interfered with psychiatric assessments, later pleading guilty to breach of trust; extradition took six years from her 2014 arrest Gerald Ridsdale (Ballarat): first report 1975, first action 1993 (18 years). Bishop Mulkearns knew by 1975 and moved him through parishes; a police officer took the bishop's promise to handle it Frank Houston (Assemblies of God): first report 1999, first action 2015 (16 years). His son Brian Houston, then national president, and the national executive did not refer the 1999 allegations to police
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Victoria 2015: Limitation period for child abuse civil claims removed (Feb 2015) New South Wales 2016: Limitation period removed (March 2016) Australian Capital Territory 2016: Limitation period removed (Aug 2016) Northern Territory 2017: Limitation period removed (June 2017) Tasmania 2017: Limitation period removed Western Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (April 2018) South Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (Sept 2018) Queensland 2018: Legislation amended (Nov 2018 per Shine); Queensland first removed the period for institutional child sexual abuse in 2016
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1997: Bringing Them Home — HREOC national inquiry (Stolen Generations).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer: Extradited January 2021; convicted 3 April 2023; Litzman took a plea deal for breach of trust and resigned from the Knesset (2022)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Australia on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1994: Crimes (Child Sex Tourism) Amendment Act 1994 in force 5 July 1994 — one of the first offender-country laws 2017: Australia: laws from 13 Dec 2017 allow cancelling passports of up to 20,000 registered child sex offenders; about 800 registered offenders had travelled abroad the previous year
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Queensland Police Task Force Argos ran the Childs Play site for about 11 months (2016–17).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report; Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7; Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry; Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions; Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia; Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale); Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care; Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling; Wood Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service — paedophile inquiry (1997); South Australia — Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, 'The Life They Deserve' (2016); Western Australia — St Andrew's Hostel Katanning special inqu.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
cases.who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cases.what: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.
cases.cover_up: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
cases.who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
cases.what: US Customs' first major case against internet child abuse material. In late 1992 a US Customs controlled delivery led to a suspect who said he had obtained images from a Europe-based bulletin board; agents found 'Bamse', a Danish bulletin board with child abuse rooms, and two other Danish boards using its images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own. Working with Danish authorities, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. Start year approximate.

cases.title: Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ballarat; Bishop Ronald Mulkearns
cases.what: Gerald Ridsdale, ordained 1961, was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children; he died in prison in 2025. He was moved between parishes including Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope and Mortlake, then to Sydney. The Royal Commission's Ballarat report of 6 December 2017 found Bishop Mulkearns knew of his offending by late 1975 and still reappointed him, a 'catastrophic' failure. It also found police obstruction of a 1972 investigation of Monsignor John Day.
cases.cover_up: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

cases.title: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
cases.who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cases.what: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cases.cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged

cases.title: Denis Chrysostom Alexander — extradition from Australia
cases.who: Benedictine monk, Fort Augustus Abbey School
cases.what: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland in the 1970s. A 2013 BBC investigation reported that after a pupil told his parents, who complained to the school, Alexander was sent back to Australia with no warning about his offending; he became a parish priest in Sydney. Scotland requested his extradition in August 2016 and he was arrested in Sydney in January 2017. After contesting extradition he was returned to Scotland in January 2020. In June 2021 at the High Court in Edinburgh he pleaded guilty to indecent behaviour against two boys aged 12 to 14 between 1973 and 1976, and on 30 July 2021 he was jailed for four years and five months.
cases.cover_up: Sent back to Australia by the school after parents complained; police not informed

cases.title: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.what: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cover_up: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

cases.title: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.what: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
cases.cover_up: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.

cases.title: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
cases.who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
cases.what: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.
cases.cover_up: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').

cases.title: Royal Commission — Catholic Church data, Australia
cases.who: Catholic Church in Australia, incl. St John of God Brothers (40.4% of brothers accused)
cases.what: Data presented to the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse on 6 February 2017 showed 4,444 people reported abuse to Catholic authorities between 1980 and 2015, at more than 1,000 institutions, naming 1,880 alleged perpetrators. About 7% of priests who served between 1950 and 2010 were alleged perpetrators; 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused. Religious brothers (32%) and priests (30%) were the largest groups. The commission referred 309 cases to police.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Tasmania — Ombudsman's review of claims of abuse in state care, 'Listen to the Children' (2004)
cases.who: Tasmanian state care: state, church and charitable homes (including Ashley, Rochebank, Clarendon, Kennerley, Glenara and Mt St Canice) and foster care
cases.what: After a former state ward spoke publicly in July 2003 about abuse in state care, the Tasmanian Ombudsman reviewed claims from adults who had been abused as children in state care, publishing 'Listen to the Children' in November 2004 and a Phase 2 final report in June 2006. The review covered state, church and charitable homes and foster care, where sexual abuse from the 1950s to the 1970s had been described. It led to the state's Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013), which accepted 1,848 claimants and paid between $35,000 and $60,000 each. Claimants who accepted a payment had to waive future legal action against the government. Tasmania's 2023 Commission of Inquiry later found that allegations against staff and carers revealed through the program had not been acted on.

cases.title: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
cases.who: Anglican Church of Australia
cases.what: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).

cases.title: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
cases.who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
cases.what: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. The order made the most compensation payments of any Catholic authority: 763, totalling A$48.5 million. In Ballarat, former Brothers Edward Dowlan and Robert Best, the principal of St Alipius school, were jailed for sexual crimes against pupils.
cases.cover_up: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades

cases.title: Australian Defence Force — HMAS Leeuwin, Balcombe and ADF Cadets (Royal Commission Case Study 40)
cases.who: Royal Australian Navy (HMAS Leeuwin), Army Apprentice School Balcombe, Australian Air Force Cadets
cases.what: The Royal Commission's Case Study 40 report (23 August 2017) found that physical and sexual abuse of child recruits was widespread at the navy base HMAS Leeuwin from the 1960s to 1972, that senior staff knew and tolerated it, and that the navy failed in its duty of care. At the Army Apprentice School, Balcombe, in the 1970s and 1980s an unofficial rank hierarchy let senior apprentices sexually and physically abuse junior ones. In the Air Force Cadets, policies from at least 2000 gave the age of consent as 14, which the commission said increased the risk of abuse. cases.title: Victoria — Board of Inquiry into historical child sexual abuse at Beaumaris Primary School and other government schools (2024)
cases.who: Victorian Department of Education; Beaumaris Primary School and 23 other government schools
cases.what: A Victorian Government Board of Inquiry, set up after reports of abuse at Beaumaris Primary School, tabled its final report in Parliament on 6 March 2024. It examined the school from 1960 to 1994 (abuse there was concentrated in 1971–72) and was widened to 23 other government schools. It focused on four teachers, out of six relevant staff, who are believed to have abused more than 100 students, mostly boys aged 9 to 12. The board found the department 'woefully failed to protect children', had no policies for handling allegations or convictions, and covered up abuse. It made nine recommendations, including a parliamentary apology and accountability processes for historical abuse in all state schools.
cases.cover_up: Board found a culture of covering up child sexual abuse in the Department of Education to protect the system's reputation; a teacher convicted and found guilty of misconduct in the 1980s was moved into administration and banned from teaching for only three years

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. flows.title: Seoul → Australia
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Australia; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → Australia child migrants
flows.what: Children in British care were sent to institutions in Australia where IICSA found a catalogue of evidence of ill-treatment and sexual abuse; the last child was migrated in 1970.

flows.title: Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's
flows.what: After complaints were quietly investigated at Brisbane Grammar in the early 1980s, counsellor Kevin Lynch later worked at St Paul's School, where he also abused students; he was charged in 1997.

flows.title: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse
flows.what: AUSTRAC alleged Westpac failed to vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines (A$1.3bn penalty, 2020); an Australian man paid a Filipino mother while directing abuse over Skype for nearly five years. IJM's 2020 study ranked Australians third among purchasers.

flows.what: Peter Scully fled Melbourne for the Philippines in 2011 and ran a pay-per-view abuse site there; life sentence 2018.

flows.title: Australia → Philippines travelling offenders
flows.what: Several Australian men have been convicted in Australia for abusing children in the Philippines, including a flight attendant who abused 26 girls from 2010 to 2017.

flows.title: Australia → Southeast Asia registered offenders' travel
flows.what: Australia's Foreign Minister said about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, with 40% not notifying police.

flows.what: After a pupil's parents complained, the abbey school sent the monk back to Australia without telling police; he was arrested in Sydney in 2017 and pleaded guilty in 2021.

flows.what: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating him; he was jailed in 2015.

flows.title: Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged)
flows.what: A Salesian priest convicted of abuse in Melbourne was allegedly moved to Samoa to avoid further police investigation.

patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2024: proposed ban: Swiss Federal Council advocates a general ban on intercountry adoption (late 2024)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban; Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. cases.title: Swiss bar owner jailed 16 years for abusing more than 80 boys in Pattaya and northern Thailand
cases.who: Unnamed Swiss national (72, from Lucerne) who ran a bar in Pattaya

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
cases.who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
cases.what: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.

cases.title: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
cases.who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
cases.what: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
cases.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.who: Catholic clergy in Ecuador

A survivors' association demanded that such crimes be made imprescriptible, as approved in a referendum.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Burundian and Gabonese peacekeepers in the Central African Republic (2016): Not charged (per Wikipedia citing UN/AP)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. patterns.role: Home country of accused troops or staff

patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi; Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities

patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019

cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students.
