cases.title: Italy — Il Forteto community, Tuscany: abuse of children placed by courts
cases.who: Il Forteto agricultural cooperative and community; Tuscany Region, juvenile court and local authorities that placed and accredited it
cases.what: Il Forteto, a cooperative and community at Vicchio in the Mugello near Florence, received children placed by juvenile courts and social services for decades. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, was definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse, although a conviction had already become final in 1985 and placements continued. Two Tuscan regional council inquiry commissions examined the case; a parliamentary inquiry in the previous legislature did not finish with a final report, and a new bicameral commission of inquiry was created by Law 47 of 25 March 2024 and installed on 1 August 2024. Its task is to establish institutional responsibilities and why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse and mistreatment.
cases.cover_up: The founder already had a final conviction in 1985, yet courts and social services kept placing children there; parliament's 2024 commission is to establish why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on sexual abuse and mistreatment.

cases.title: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
cases.who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
cases.what: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
cases.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
cases.what: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone (South Tyrol)
cases.what: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its 631-page report on 20 January 2025, described as the first fully independent study of its kind in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven and was removed only in 2010. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a general and highly systemic failure. Bishop Ivo Muser said 'every case is one too many' and that victims' suffering should fill the church with shame.
cases.cover_up: Handling of abuse cases until 2010 was a systemic failure; one priest was removed only in 2010 despite allegations from the 1960s.

cases.title: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
cases.who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
cases.what: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were made to believe their babies had died, and given for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff and organisations operating outside hospitals, and noted that private intermediaries were paid for their role. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report on 4 October 2019 by 88 votes with 13 abstentions.
cases.cover_up: Some hospitals did not register or destroyed birth records from 1970 onward (e.g. Carlos Van Buren hospital, Valparaíso); the commission also found gaps in birth and departure records

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) — national safeguarding reports (2022–2025)
cases.who: Conferenza Episcopale Italiana — diocesan listening centres and the national child-protection service
cases.what: The Italian Bishops' Conference published its first national report in November 2022, prepared with experts of the Università Cattolica: 80 diocesan listening centres had received 86 contacts in 2020–2021 concerning 89 people, against 68 alleged abusers, 44% of them clerics. CEI also said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican's doctrine office since 2000. Its third survey, presented in May 2025, counted 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) and 67 alleged perpetrators, 44 of them clergy, in 2023–2024. Critics said the reports are too narrow and Italy has no independent national inquiry.
cases.cover_up: Critics, including Rete l'Abuso, said the reports cover only recent diocesan-desk data and omit court and Vatican cases; the first report mentions no reports to civil authorities.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
cases.who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
cases.what: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

cases.title: Operation Chemosh — minors sharing abuse 'stickers' in WhatsApp groups
cases.who: Encrypted chat groups, many members minors
cases.what: Begun in 2017 after a public report about children forming WhatsApp groups to create and exchange abuse material, including emoji 'stickers'. Thirty-three investigations were opened (26 in Spain) with arrests in Spain, Italy and France; the average age of those arrested in Spain was 22 because many were minors.

cases.title: Operation Sky — Skype group sharing abuse material
cases.who: Invitation-only Skype group with members from 14 countries
cases.what: Spanish police followed Tor links to a private Skype group whose members from 14 countries exchanged abuse material; by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada.

cases.title: IOM: up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy may be sex-trafficking victims
cases.who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
cases.what: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
cases.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

cases.title: Germany, Spain, Italy, Greece — romance-method pimps, Nigerian networks, unaccompanied children (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: 'Loverboy' traffickers; Nigerian cult-linked groups; Eastern European recruiters
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say young male traffickers in Germany and Spain coerce girls into sex trafficking through sham romantic relationships; highly organized groups sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations exploit Nigerian women and girls in Germany and Italy, in Italy through debt and 'voodoo' rituals; Eastern European girls are recruited online for child sex trafficking in Italy; and in Greece unaccompanied children are vulnerable to sex trafficking and Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg.

flows.title: Seoul → Italy
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Italy; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Bucharest → Italy
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Italy in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Edo State → Libya → Italy (sex trafficking of women and girls)
flows.what: Women and girls, most from Edo State, are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and oaths. IOM recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims arriving by sea in 2014–2017.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
flows.what: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.

flows.title: Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019)
flows.what: Indicted in Arizona in 2003, the Salvatorian priest went to Italy and evaded a confirmed extradition until his arrest in Rome in May 2019.

flows.title: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi
flows.what: Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)
networks.what: Nigerian confraternity whose members in Italy were arrested in 2016 for 'mafia conspiracy, drug trafficking, exploitation of prostitution and violent crimes'. A Palermo court convicted 14 in 2018; in 2019 another Palermo court rejected the mafia-association charge for five others.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2001: moratorium: United States suspends adoptions from Cambodia (late 2001) 2004: conviction: Lauryn Galindo pleads guilty in US to visa fraud and money-laundering conspiracy over Cambodian adoptions
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 1996: Cambodia: 1996 Law on Suppression of the Kidnapping, Trafficking and Exploitation of Human Persons 2002: Svay Pak (Phnom Penh): child prostitution "bustling", driven by Western child-sex tourism after child prostitution in Thailand was cracked down upon 2003: 22 January 2003 police raid on Svay Pak child brothels — widely advertised in advance; no arrests; nearly all children moved beforehand to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. A Dateline NBC–IJM operation later in 2003 rescued 37 girls 2005: Cambodian government shut down Svay Pak brothels (2005); by 2006 prostitutes "no longer operate[d] with impunity"; 2008 Dateline: brothels "moved out of town"; 2011 CNN: trade had gone underground 2008: Cambodia: Law on Suppression of Human Trafficking and Sexual Exploitation (2008)
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001; Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations; UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers; Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline; Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
cases.who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
cases.what: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. Released in February 2023, he was recalled to prison in March 2023 for breaching licence conditions.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Operation Twisted Traveler — ICE crackdown on US offenders in Cambodia (2009)
cases.who: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement; Cambodian police
cases.what: In August 2009 three previously convicted US sex offenders arrested by Cambodian police in February — Ronald Boyajian, Erik Peeters and Jack Sporich — were returned to Los Angeles as the first defendants charged under 'Operation Twisted Traveler'. ICE head John Morton called Cambodia 'ground zero for child sex tourism'; ICE had stationed an agent in Cambodia full-time. Peeters was accused of abusing at least three Cambodian boys and Sporich of abusing a boy in Siem Reap (accusations at the time).

cases.title: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
cases.who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
cases.what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.
cases.cover_up: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.

cases.title: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
cases.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
cases.what: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.

cases.title: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
cases.who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
cases.what: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. After crackdowns by the government, police and international agencies, open street sales ended and the trade moved to more hidden venues such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.
cases.cover_up: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.

cases.title: Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.
cases.cover_up: The report says official complicity, including at senior levels, inhibited effective law enforcement.

flows.title: Phnom Penh → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Phnom Penh, FY1994–FY2008 (peak 407 in FY2001).

flows.title: Phnom Penh → United States
flows.what: About 800 Cambodian children adopted to US families through Lauryn Galindo, convicted on visa-fraud and money-laundering charges in 2004.

flows.title: United States → Cambodia (travelling child sex offenders)
flows.what: US men, several already convicted at home, travelled repeatedly to Cambodia to buy children; prosecuted in Los Angeles under the PROTECT Act.

flows.title: Vietnam → Svay Pak, Cambodia (girls sold to brothels)
flows.what: Most children in Svay Pak brothels were ethnic Vietnamese, many sold by destitute families; US TIP 2025 still reports ethnic Vietnamese women and girls exploited in Cambodian cities and tourist areas.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

networks.name: Operation Yewtree (UK entertainment figures)
networks.what: Metropolitan Police investigation opened 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations; 19 arrests and 7 convictions of entertainment figures.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2000: Saeima (Latvian parliament) investigation commission on the paedophilia case, and the Prosecutor General's finding that its claims were false (2000).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2022: law: Latvia law preventing adoptions to the US takes effect (1 July 2022, per US FY2024 report)

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Latvia — Logos Centrs child exploitation network, Riga (1999–2002 convictions)
cases.who: Logos Centrs video and model agency, Riga (director Jurijs Jurjevs)
cases.what: After a September 1999 Latvian TV report, prosecutors investigated the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by Jurijs Jurjevs, which The Baltic Times described as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring; seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and sentenced to ten years, the maximum; pageant agency manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years; Ingus Tūns' case was tried separately. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, Jurjevs received more than four years and Tūns five. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and found false (see the Saeima commission record).

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false
cases.who: Saeima investigation commission chaired by MP Jānis Ādamsons; former PM Andris Šķēle, ex-justice minister Valdis Birkavs, State Revenue Service head Andrejs Sončiks (accused, cleared)
cases.what: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who on 17 February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission about them was false. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander; in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats. None of the officials was charged.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
cases.who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
cases.what: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. The order made the most compensation payments of any Catholic authority: 763, totalling A$48.5 million. In Ballarat, former Brothers Edward Dowlan and Robert Best, the principal of St Alipius school, were jailed for sexual crimes against pupils.
cases.cover_up: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades

cases.title: Senate 'Lost Innocents' — child migrants abused in Australian institutions (2001)
cases.who: Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia (Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf, Tardun) and other receiving institutions for British and Maltese child migrants
cases.what: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Lost Innocents: Righting the Record — Report on child migration' in August 2001. Of 207 former child migrants who made submissions, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

cases.title: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010
cases.who: Catholic Church in Malta — Response Team set up by the Maltese bishops (chair Judge Victor Caruana Colombo)
cases.what: In April 2010 the Maltese Curia said the Church's Response Team, set up by the bishops in 1991 and chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 remained open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 3,263 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram. Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram. Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020). Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Where children are abused for paying viewers

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
cases.who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
cases.what: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.

cases.title: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
cases.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
cases.what: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.

cases.title: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
cases.who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.

cases.title: Oba of Benin revokes trafficking 'juju' oaths (March 2018)
cases.who: Oba of Benin, Ewuare II; Edo traditional priests
cases.what: In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, publicly revoked the curses that juju priests had used to bind trafficking victims to their traffickers and laid a curse on anyone involved in trafficking within his domain. Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in September 2018 that anecdotal evidence suggested trafficking had slowed, and cited UNODC that at least nine in ten Nigerian women trafficked to Europe come from Edo State.

cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men
cases.who: Imam Ahmad Bun Hambal Centre for Islamic Studies (purported Islamic school / rehabilitation centre)
cases.what: On 26 September 2019 Kaduna police raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many chained and with whip scars. Some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana; families said they were denied access. Seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested. Local media reported captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused. The raid led to further rescues from similar 'torture houses' in northern Nigeria.

cases.title: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
cases.who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
cases.what: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).

cases.title: IOM: up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy may be sex-trafficking victims
cases.who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
cases.what: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

cases.title: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
cases.who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
cases.what: On the night of Friday 11 December 2020 heavily armed gunmen raided the all-boys Government Science Secondary School in Kankara, Katsina state, where more than 800 students lived. The military said 333 pupils were unaccounted for. In an audio message a man identifying himself as Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction; Nigerian officials attributed it to bandits, and the BBC later described a local gang leader as the mastermind of the kidnapping of about 300 boys. The boys were freed within about a week.

cases.title: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram (JAS)
cases.what: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest. Amnesty International said on the tenth anniversary in April 2024 that 82 girls remained in captivity and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former Boko Haram fighters; in April 2015 it estimated that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since the start of 2014.

cases.title: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
cases.what: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.

cases.title: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
cases.who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
cases.what: On the evening of 19 February 2018 militants stormed Dapchi, Yobe state, and abducted girls from a boarding school; Nigeria's government said 110 schoolgirls were missing. On 21 March 2018 the government said 106 children — 104 schoolgirls, a girl who did not attend the school and a boy — had been freed, and denied paying a ransom. Five girls were reported to have died during the journey after the abduction. The only Christian girl in the group, who refused to convert, remained in captivity.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites
cases.who: Trafficking networks supplying mining camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. It also reports some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and to a lesser extent Cap Skirring and La Petite Côte.

cases.title: Côte d'Ivoire — girls brought to Abidjan for domestic servitude; Nigerian girls at mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Relatives and Nigerian trafficking networks
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan for school or training and then exploit them in domestic servitude, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; Ivorian women and girls are sex-trafficked especially in Abidjan; and Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls for shop jobs then exploit them in gold-mining and cocoa regions.

flows.title: Abuja → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Abuja, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 197 in FY2012).

flows.title: Chibok → Sambisa Forest: abducted schoolgirls
flows.what: Girls were driven or marched away, possibly to the Konduga area of the Sambisa Forest where Boko Haram had fortified camps; military sources believed they were split among camps around Lake Chad, the Gorsi mountains and Sambisa.

flows.title: Sextortion: Nigeria-based offenders ← US teenage victims
flows.what: Lagos-based offenders demanded money from US teenagers after obtaining images; the Ogoshi brothers targeted hundreds of US teenagers and adults (DOJ).

flows.title: Edo State → Libya → Italy (sex trafficking of women and girls)
flows.what: Women and girls, most from Edo State, are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and oaths. IOM recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims arriving by sea in 2014–2017.

flows.title: Nigeria → gold-mining regions of Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire
flows.what: Organized networks transport Nigerian women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire for sex trafficking; in Kédougou victims include girls as young as 12.

flows.title: Burkina Faso / Mali / Ghana → Kaduna: children held in purported Islamic school
flows.what: Police said some of the 300+ captives freed in the 2019 Kaduna raid had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana.

networks.name: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)
networks.what: Facilities posing as maternity homes, clinics or orphanages where pregnant girls and women are held (some raped) and their babies sold, including for illegal adoption. Raids: Enugu 2008, Aba 2011 (32 girls), Ihiala 2011, Imo 2013, Lagos 2018 (162 children).

networks.name: Islamic State (ISIS / Da'esh)
networks.what: ISIS abducted thousands of Yazidi women and children from Sinjar in August 2014 and ran markets for their sale; the UN COI found genocide. Affiliates in West Africa, the Sahel and Mozambique are verified by the UN as abducting children.

networks.name: Boko Haram (JAS) and ISWAP
networks.what: Abducted 276 schoolgirls at Chibok (2014) and 110 at Dapchi (2018); UN verified 991 child abductions and 419 cases of sexual violence through forced marriage in Nigeria in 2024. Active across the Lake Chad basin.

networks.name: Nigeria-based financial sextortion
networks.what: Offenders posing as young women on social media extort teenage boys for money; NCMEC counts at least three dozen US teenage boys who died by suicide after financial sextortion since 2021 (all offender nationalities).

networks.name: Sextortion targeting children (general)
networks.what: Placeholder grouping for individual sextortion prosecutions; IWF: 92% of sextortion reports it assessed 2023–2025 involved boys.

networks.name: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)
networks.what: Nigerian confraternity whose members in Italy were arrested in 2016 for 'mafia conspiracy, drug trafficking, exploitation of prostitution and violent crimes'. A Palermo court convicted 14 in 2018; in 2019 another Palermo court rejected the mafia-association charge for five others.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Panama — legislative subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)

cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. cases.title: Senegal — forced begging and abuse of talibé children in Quranic schools (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Some marabouts (Quranic teachers) running residential daaras
cases.what: Human Rights Watch and the Senegalese PPDH platform reported on 11 June 2019 that over 100,000 talibé children in Senegal are forced by some Quranic teachers to beg daily, often under quotas enforced by beatings. For 2017–2018 they documented 16 deaths of talibés from beatings, neglect or endangerment, 61 cases of beatings, 15 cases of actual or attempted rape or sexual abuse and 14 cases of children chained or imprisoned, in 8 of Senegal's 14 regions. The 2025 US TIP report says the government identified 573 child forced-begging victims in the year.

cases.title: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. cases.title: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
patterns.role_note: At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims; Catholic, insurance and Scouts lobbying against limitation reform is documented in several states.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.
